title: The midwives (Exodus 1)
hookLine: Shiphrah and Puah refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the boys

lines: A KING WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH.
cards: Exodus opens with a list of names, Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt, and then the family grows until the land is full of them. Then one quiet, chilling line: a new king arose over Egypt who knew not Joseph.

All the grain, all the lives saved, forgotten in a generation. The new king sees this growing people as a threat. He puts them to forced labor, building store cities, making bricks, working the fields.
And they keep growing. So he tries something worse, with an order for two women who deliver babies: the first in Exodus to tell Pharaoh no.

teach.h: IF IT'S A BOY, KILL HIM.
teach.b: The order: when you help the Hebrew women give birth, if it's a boy, kill him; if it's a girl, let her live. Then the refusal.
The text says it simply: "But the midwives feared God." They let the boys live. Fear here isn't panic but reverence: they stood in awe of God more than of the most powerful man they'd ever meet.
Then the excuse. Pharaoh calls them back: why have you done this?

teach.h: THEY'RE QUICK; WE COME TOO LATE.
teach.b: With a straight face they answer that Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women; they're vigorous, and they give birth before the midwife even gets there. A clever answer, maybe a sly one, and it keeps them alive.

teach.h: THE MIDWIVES ARE NAMED. PHARAOH ISN'T.
teach.b: The midwives are named: Shiphrah and Puah, which the Douay-Rheims spells Sephora and Phua. The king of Egypt never gets a name at all.

God dealt well with the midwives, the text says, and gave them households of their own. Nobody knows for sure whether they were Hebrew women or Egyptian women who served the Hebrews; the Hebrew can be read either way.
The Church has long honored this kind of courage. Its Catechism says a citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow orders of civil authorities that go against the moral order.
Peter put it in one line in Acts: "We ought to obey God, rather than men." Two women in a birthing room said it first. The chapter ends darkly: Pharaoh orders every newborn boy thrown into the Nile.

how: Catholic teaching on conscience holds that a person must refuse a command from any authority that would require a grave wrong, and Catholic writers on the defense of life often point to Shiphrah and Puah as early examples.

games.q: you're Shiphrah. you've let the boys live, and now Pharaoh has called you in: why have you done this? what do you say?
o: confess you disobeyed him on purpose.
tell him the Hebrew women give birth before you can get there.
promise you'll obey from now on.
games.why: they tell him the Hebrew women are vigorous and deliver before the midwife comes. it keeps them alive, and the text says God dealt well with them.

practice: Most of us will never face a Pharaoh, but small orders come all day: pass along the rumor, fudge the number, laugh at the joke about someone who isn't there, look away.

Picture one you're likely to meet, then picture yourself quietly not doing it, just a no. If you pray, ask for the midwives' kind of courage; if you don't, rehearse that no until it feels like your own.

wordCard.voice: The midwives. Shiphrah and Puah, who feared God more than Pharaoh, and let the Hebrew boys live. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shiphrah, a name often explained as beautiful or fair. the Douay-Rheims spells her Sephora.
